summary: The article reports on a visit to Meadow Valley Community College (MVCC) on October 15, 2023, showing how community colleges are drawing a growing number of adult learners, from mid-career professionals to retirees. It covers MVCC's adult courses, flexible scheduling, support services like subsidized childcare, employer partnerships, technology training, and efforts to reduce the stigma around adult education. Student stories and staff and employer quotes illustrate the impact.
one_line: Meadow Valley Community College's flexible, well-supported adult education programs are helping adult learners change careers and challenging the stigma around learning later in life.
key_facts: The author visited Meadow Valley Community College (MVCC) on October 15, 2023, describing it as a forerunner in adult education.
Dr. Emily Carter, head of MVCC's Adult Education Department, said "Learning is a lifelong endeavor."
MVCC's adult offerings range from basic literacy programs to advanced technical courses, including a certification in healthcare administration.
James Peterson, a 58-year-old former warehouse supervisor, returned to school after a layoff and is close to graduating with an associate degree in logistics management.
Maria Gonzalez, a single mother of two, completed her GED at MVCC and then enrolled in the nursing program, calling MVCC "a lifeline."
MVCC offers evening and weekend classes, online coursework, and short-term certificate programs to suit working adults.
Kevin Thompson, a software developer, is enrolled in an advanced cybersecurity certification program and values the online and evening options.
MVCC provides childcare services, career counseling, and financial aid assistance as support for adult learners.
On September 12, MVCC launched a partnership with local daycares to provide subsidized childcare for students, according to Lisa Hamilton, head of student support services.
Bob Sanders, CEO of TechInnovate, an IT company that frequently hires MVCC graduates, said they bring "a unique perspective and maturity" to their roles.
Susan Wu, a professor in MVCC's Digital Media program, stresses keeping technology skills current at any age.
Gregory Adams, a recent retiree in a creative writing course, said "Learning doesn't stop when you hit a certain age."
MVCC works with local businesses to align curriculum with market demands and create post-graduation employment pathways.
